opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started from my own frustration. When I was trying to get a visa appointment, the slots would open up at random times and disappear within minutes. Refreshing the website by hand all day was exhausting, so I wrote a small script that checked availability and notified me when something opened up.

Once it worked for me, I realized many other students were going through the exact same pain, especially international students who needed to get back to school or start an internship on time. Keeping it to myself didn't make sense. The code wasn't complicated, and the value came from more people being able to use it, not from me holding onto it.

I've also always been a big believer in open source. A lot of what I learned as a student came from reading other people's code on GitHub, so putting something useful back out there felt natural. And once it's public, others can fix bugs, adapt it when the website changes, or extend it to other consulates, which a single person could never keep up with.

So it was really "I solved my own problem, and it costs me nothing to help others solve theirs." Seeing people message me saying it helped them get an appointment was one of the most rewarding parts.

r001.rationale: He says he realized many other students were going through the same problem he had, so keeping the working tool to himself did not make sense.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started from pure frustration. I was trying to get a US visa appointment, and the earliest slot was something like a year out. So I did what any lazy engineer does: I wrote a little script that polled the appointment site and rescheduled me the moment something earlier opened up. It worked. I got a date months sooner than I would have otherwise.

And then I sat there thinking, this is a problem that thousands of students and workers are dealing with right now, and most of them aren't going to write a scraper at two in the morning. Some of them were paying hundreds of dollars to shady "agents" who were basically running the same kind of bot. That felt wrong to me. The information was public, the technique was trivial, and the only thing gating access was whether you happened to know how to code.

So open-sourcing it was partly about fairness. If a tool like this exists, I'd rather it exist for everyone than for a small group who can afford to pay for it. And partly it was just the way I've always worked. I came up in the reinforcement learning community, where I helped build Tianshou and worked on OpenAI Gym, and that culture is very much "if you built something useful, put it on GitHub." Someone else will find a bug, someone will add support for another country, someone will port it to a different consulate's system. That all happened, by the way. People extended it in ways I never would have.

I'll say there was a real tension, though. If too many people hammer the booking site, it degrades for everyone, and it can get accounts flagged. So I tried to be responsible about defaults, like polling intervals, and I was pretty upfront in the README about not being a jerk with it. I don't think the answer to "this could be misused" is to keep it secret. The answer is to document it well and trust people to use it sensibly.

r001.rationale: He says he realized thousands of students and workers faced the same appointment problem he had, motivating him to make the tool available to everyone.

astra-6.text: I wanted to make the process a little less frustrating. Checking for visa appointments over and over is repetitive, and a scraper can help with that. Making it open source meant other people could use it, see how it worked, and adapt it to their own needs. It felt like something that would be more useful shared than kept to myself.

r001.rationale: The response says others could use or adapt the scraper, but does not say Jiayi inferred they shared his own need for it.
